entities.summary:
The Battle of Bannockburn was a pivotal event in the First War of Scottish Independence, fought on July 1-2, 1314, in Bannockburn, Scotland. This battle saw the forces of King Robert the Bruce, led by Sir James Douglas and Sir Thomas Randolph, decisively defeat the English army under King Edward II, led by Sir Henry de Bohun. The outcome of the battle was a crushing defeat for the English, with over 1000 soldiers killed and many more captured. The victory at Bannockburn was a significant turning point in the war, as it secured a major victory for the Scots and paved the way for the eventual signing of the Declaration of Arbroath in 1320, which asserted Scotland's independence from England.

The battle itself was marked by a series of brutal and bloody skirmishes between the two armies, with both sides suffering heavy casualties. The English army, which was led by the experienced knight Sir Henry de Bohun, was ultimately defeated by the brave and determined Scots, who were led by King Robert the Bruce and his trusted generals. The battle was a testament to the bravery and determination of the Scottish people, who were fighting for their freedom and independence from their English overlords.

The Battle of Bannockburn is remembered as one of the greatest victories in Scottish history, and its legacy continues to be celebrated to this day. The battle's significance extends beyond Scotland, as it marked a major turning point in the history of the British Isles and paved the way for the eventual rise of the Kingdom of Scotland as a major power in Europe.
